abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a fundamental reconceptualization of knowledge representation through the Contextual Situation Calculus (CSC), a novel formalism that treats contexts as first-class ontological entities rather than mere annotations. Traditional approaches to reasoning about actions and change face significant limitations when modeling agents operating in dynamically evolving, multi-perspective environments where the same facts may have different truth values across contexts. Our theoretical framework introduces hierarchical context structures with well-founded semantics, enabling agents to maintain coherent reasoning across disparate epistemic states while preserving the advantages of classical logic-based approaches. We establish the formal properties of CSC, proving soundness and completeness results for the proposed inference mechanisms. The paradigm innovation lies in our treatment of context relations as explicit, manipulable objects within the knowledge base, allowing for systematic reasoning about perspective shifts, context embeddings, and cross-context inference. Complexity analysis demonstrates that our approach remains within the same computational complexity class as classicalsituation calculus while enabling significantly richer expressivity. We further provide a translation methodology from existing knowledge representation formalisms to CSC, facilitating adoption and interoperability. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for context-sensitive reasoning in artificial intelligence, with implications for automated reasoning, cognitive modeling, and intelligent agent design.

We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of heuristic search in classical planning that yields substantial improvements over existing methods. While planning heuristics based on delete Relaxation have demonstrated empirical success, their theoretical properties and inherent limitations remain incompletely understood. This paper establishes novel theoretical results characterizing the relationship between relaxation-based heuristics and plan quality, providing formal proofs that explain observed empirical phenomena and identifying conditions under which these heuristics are guaranteed to produce bounded suboptimal solutions. We introduce the concept of relevance graphs to characterize structural properties of planning problems that affect heuristic accuracy, and prove that our refined analysis enables construction of tighter admissible heuristics through selective relaxation. Our main theoretical contribution is the derivation of error bounds for delete relaxation heuristics that depend on problem-specific parameters rather than worst-case instances, significantly improving upon previous general bounds. Furthermore, we prove that combining multiple relaxation variants using a novel weighting scheme yields heuristics with strictly better worst-case performance than any individual relaxation. These theoretical findings translate into practical improvements: we demonstrate that planning systems employing our theoretically grounded heuristic formulations solve problems with up to 40% fewer node expansions while guaranteeing solution quality bounds. This work bridges the gap between theoretical analysis and practical planning algorithm design.

We present Neuro-Symbolic Autonomous Robotic Agents (NSARA), a novel system architecture that fundamentally reconceptualizes how robotic systems integrate neural perception with symbolic reasoning. Current approaches to robotic planning typically treat perception and reasoning as separate pipeline stages, leading to brittleness when handling novel situations and limiting the depth of planning that can be performed in real-time. NSARA introduces a differentiable neural-symbolic interface that enables seamless gradient flow between learned perception modules and symbolic planning components, allowing each to inform and improve the other during both training and execution. The system architecture features a learned perceptual grounding layer that maps raw sensor observations to symbolic representations, a constraint-aware symbolic planner operating over these grounded representations, and a metacognitive module that monitors planning performance and triggers perception refinement when reasoning fails. This paradigm shift toward tightly integrated neural-symbolic processing enables NSARA to handle partial observability and ambiguous situations more robustly than previous systems while performing hierarchical planning with temporal depths previously unachievable in real-time robotic applications. Extensive evaluation across manipulation, navigation, and collaborative tasks demonstrates that NSARA achieves 73% higher success rates on novel task variations compared to state-of-the-art baselines while requiring 60% less training data through the proposed neuro-symbolic integration.

We introduce Adaptive Multi-scale Language Understanding (AMSLU), a transformer-based system architecture that substantially advances the state of the art in natural language processing through novel hierarchical attention mechanisms and efficient dynamic computation. Existing large language models process all inputs with uniform computational allocation, leading to inefficiencies when handling variable complexity inputs and limitations in capturing discourse-level phenomena. AMSLU addresses these shortcomings through a multi-scale attention architecture that simultaneously processes text at character, subword, word, and sentence levels, with dynamic routing mechanisms that allocate computational resources based on input complexity. The system incorporates learned complexity predictors that enable selective activation of deeper reasoning layers only when necessary, achieving significant improvements in inference efficiency. Our architectural innovations include cross-scale attention pathways that enable direct information flow between different granularity levels and a novel positional encoding scheme that captures both absolute and relative positional relationships across scales. Evaluation on comprehensive benchmarks spanning question answering, summarization, and natural language inference demonstrates that AMSLU achieves new state-of-the-art performance with 35% fewer parameters than comparable systems. Furthermore, the dynamic computation mechanism reduces average inference latency by 52% while maintaining full-model quality on complex reasoning tasks, making the system suitable for real-time applications. Ablation studies validate the contribution of each architectural component.
